solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Box contains one b—– big key

indicators.note: contains tells us the word for box holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: to box is to spar
an ace is a one on dice or cards
the b is taken as the letter B

explanation.surface: A boxed set holds a single item and a very large key, as if inventorying a toolkit.
explanation.definitionFit: The bar along the bottom of a keyboard is its biggest key.

clue.text: Coffee drunk with lady.. time for love (so it's assumed)

indicators.note: drunk suggests the letters are reeling about into a new order
time for love says one letter stands in place of another

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scores, the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone takes coffee with a lady and assumes romance is next on the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'time for love' swaps the O in COFFEE for T, giving CTFFEE LADY; 'drunk' then rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in a put-on, pretended manner means the manner is assumed rather than genuine.

clue.text: Although quite sensible, Henry's rampant

parts.note: someone quite sensible is no twit, written as one run of letters
the henry is the unit of inductance, symbol H
in heraldry a rampant beast is standing on its hind legs

explanation.surface: A man called Henry is out of control despite being perfectly level-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quite sensible' gives NO TWIT; 'rampant' is the heraldic word for an animal reared up, i.e. standing.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are conjunctions of concession, introducing a fact despite which something holds.

clue.text: Tablets taken orally for relief

indicators.note: taken orally, like pills swallowed, here means the word is spoken

parts.note: E is slang for an ecstasy tablet, so tablets are Es

explanation.surface: Swallowing pills to get relief from pain.
explanation.definitionFit: Relief from pain or strain is a state of comfort, a synonym.

clue.text: Stirring words from Duffy?

parts.note: Carol Ann Duffy, a former Poet Laureate, writes verse that moves the reader

explanation.surface: Praise for a rousing speech by someone named Duffy.
explanation.walkthrough: Carol Ann Duffy was the UK Poet Laureate; her moving verse is literally verse in motion, while the phrase normally means something graceful.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes anything beautifully fluid; read literally it is moving verse from a poet.

clue.text: Natural rower's position sometimes attracting comment

indicators.note: attracting comment implies the words are spoken out, so we go by sound

parts.note: a rower sits in an eight, a racing boat

explanation.surface: A rower's seat in the boat that sometimes gets people talking.
explanation.definitionFit: Inborn qualities come naturally, so natural and inborn are synonyms.

clue.text: Decides that's pointless

parts.note: having no points is zero, O
PTS is the usual abbreviation of points

explanation.surface: Someone concludes that an exercise is futile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pointless' is read as nought points: O PTS.
explanation.definitionFit: To choose between options is to decide, a synonym.

clue.text: Seeing dictator on the warpath, make exit as one

indicators.note: a dictator on the warpath is rampaging, so these letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: Spotting a furious tyrant, people flee together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make exit' reads as running away; actually 'Exit' is itself an instruction printed in a script.
explanation.definitionFit: The script instruction Exit is a typical example of what an actor is told in a play.

clue.text: Have casual sex as gigolo often demonstrates

parts.note: the word for a jester, turned round, spans the end of gigolo and the start of often

explanation.surface: A kept man's typical behaviour is sleeping around.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as an instruction, the answer says: take a jester's word and turn it round. That is exactly what 'gigoLO OFten' shows when read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb is an informal idiom for casual, uncommitted sexual dalliance.

clue.text: Spades no good — dynamite ultimately used making hole

parts.note: S abbreviates spades in card games
crap is slang for worthless

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of dynamite

explanation.surface: Digging with spades failed, so explosives were used to make the hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a hole means being in a predicament, a tight spot.

clue.text: Accept consuming passion for bird

indicators.note: consuming means the first word swallows the second

parts.note: to wear something is to tolerate or accept it
heat is intense passion, the heat of the moment

explanation.surface: Advice to give in to an all-consuming love for someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A small migratory songbird of open country, a species name.

clue.text: See you shortly at Cannes? No, beat it, punk!

indicators.note: punk means rotten or worthless, so the letters are spoilt into a new order

explanation.surface: A French farewell met by a rude brush-off telling a punk to go away.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase is said in parting, meaning until soon, as in Cannes on the Riviera.

clue.text: Checks talking books are sold here

indicators.note: talking means the clue word is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to foil a plan is to check or thwart it

explanation.surface: Checking out audiobooks in a shop that sells them.
explanation.walkthrough: FOYLES is a famous London bookshop on Charing Cross Road.
explanation.definitionFit: The bookshop is a place where books are bought, so it fits the descriptive phrase.

clue.text: Spirit guide, if seen, is way in

indicators.note: in places the street abbreviation inside the rearranged letters
to guide is to steer, so these letters are steered into a new arrangement

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A spirit guide, once seen, offers a way into the beyond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit guide' looks like one phrase from a séance, but 'guide' is the anagram signal and 'Spirit' alone the definition, in its sense of pluck.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirit as in pluck or spunk, a lively readiness to fight back.

clue.text: Groom used to rue riding under this rule

indicators.note: to groom is to arrange, tidying these letters into a new order

parts.note: SETTER'S SLIP: the printed rue has a U where the anagram needs a second E; read as REE

explanation.surface: A bridegroom regrets the custom under which a lord took his bride first.
explanation.walkthrough: Setter's slip: 'Groom' rearranges USED TO RUE RIDING, but that has two Us and two Es where the answer needs one U and three Es.
explanation.definitionFit: The supposed medieval right of a lord to bed a vassal's bride was a feudal privilege, a rule.

clue.text: Rocky northerly island not initially accessible

parts.note: Unst in Shetland is the most northerly inhabited British island

indicators.note: not initially means the first letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: something accessible is ready to hand

explanation.surface: A remote northern island that is hard to reach, with rocky shores.
explanation.definitionFit: A rocky table or chair wobbles, so rocky means wobbly here.

clue.text: Run around — why following like sheep?

indicators.note: following places the letter for why after the others

parts.note: to flee is to run away
C abbreviates circa, around
the letter Y sounds like the word why

explanation.surface: Someone asks why people follow the crowd like sheep, and tells them to run.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheep are covered in woolly fleece, so like sheep means woolly.

clue.text: Magazine entertaining old boys

indicators.note: entertaining means hosting, so the two boys hold the abbreviation for old between them

parts.note: two boys: a lad, then Ed, a boy's name

explanation.surface: A publication that amuses retired former pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: LOADED was a British lads' magazine of the 1990s; the second boy is a name, Ed.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of a well-known British men's lifestyle publication, so this is a specific example.

clue.text: Bottom you once pinched in cinema

indicators.note: pinched means the first word grips the second inside it

parts.note: arse is British slang for bottom
thou is an old form of you

explanation.surface: Someone once had their backside pinched at the pictures.
explanation.definitionFit: A cinema showing independent or foreign films, a particular kind of picture house.

clue.text: Prisoners now fitting in better

indicators.note: in puts the word for fitting inside the word for better

parts.note: someone cured is better after illness
apt means fitting or suitable

explanation.surface: Inmates are adjusting better to life inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Those now held as prisoners have been seized, taken by captors.

clue.text: Right time for storm

parts.note: an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: The ideal moment arrives for a tempest.
explanation.definitionFit: To storm is to rant furiously, a verb synonym.

clue.text: A quarter weren't particularly well secured

parts.note: a quarter of the compass is a cardinal point, here N for north
people who ailed were unwell

explanation.surface: A quarter of the group were somewhat under the weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Fixed firmly in place, fastened with nails, hence made secure.

clue.text: Really want special effects

parts.note: to really want something is to be longing for it

explanation.surface: A film fan craving spectacular special effects.
explanation.walkthrough: 'special effects' looks like one phrase but splits: 'effects' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Personal effects are one's possessions, a formal synonym.

clue.text: Country's leaders wanting for nothing

indicators.note: leaders wanting means the opening letters are missing

parts.note: Canada is a country

explanation.surface: A nation's rulers going without anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish for nothing, used in English slang for zilch.
